summary:
Embergrid is a web app for exploring satellite fire detections and comparing monthly activity across years. It addresses the MODIS and VIIRS harmonization challenge by putting both records on a common grid and testing whether district-level adjustments make earlier MODIS counts more comparable with observed VIIRS counts. The calendar labels estimates and withholds them where the adjustment fails validation.

In a held-out test covering 735 Indian districts in 2024 and 2025, the selected methods reduced average error against VIIRS by about 37%, although error increased in lower-activity months. Users can explore the Indian district calendar or use the India and world maps to inspect individual detections.

Preserving the older record gives fire managers and researchers more seasons to compare when investigating unusual activity, even as the satellites used to observe it change.
details:
Embergrid is an interactive web app for exploring historical satellite fire detections. It addresses the transition from MODIS to VIIRS by giving users a way to compare monthly fire activity across years, even though the two sensors differ in spatial resolution, sensitivity, and observation schedules.

For the India calendar, we assign NASA FIRMS detections to districts and count grid cells with at least one detection per sensor and month. We use overlapping observations to test district-specific adjustments to earlier MODIS counts. The calendar shows observed VIIRS values when available, labels historical estimates, and withholds estimates when the adjustment fails our validation check. In a held-out benchmark covering 735 districts in 2024 and 2025, the selected methods reduced mean absolute error against VIIRS from 17.22 to 10.92 occupied cells overall. Error increased in lower-activity months, so the benefit varies with activity level.

Users can select a district, compare the same month across years, and open the map to inspect individual detections. The World Hotspot Explorer uses the published Fire Harmony dataset for its global monthly series and lets users explore countries and available subdivisions on a globe or detailed map.

We built Embergrid with Python, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We used DuckDB to query archived data, Shapely and H3 for spatial processing, and Leaflet, CesiumJS, and Three.js for the maps and landing scene. The project uses archived satellite observations and requires no custom hardware.

Embergrid helps fire managers and researchers put an unusually active month in historical context and decide where to investigate further. Satellite fire masks are still needed to verify usable observation coverage. Fire cause and burned area require additional evidence.
